title: ASX slides for second week amid sell-off in local banks
excerpt: High oil prices, US bond market concerns and a sell-off in local banks drove the index lower.
body:
The ASX closed lower for the second week in a row, dragged down by high oil prices, US bond-market concerns, and a sharp sell-off in the major banks.

Our take: the bank sell-off is the more interesting part of this story. CBA and Westpac are now trading at 18 to 20 times forward earnings, down from 22 to 24 times a year ago. The market is pricing in net interest margin compression as deposits reprice up faster than loans. The dividend yields on the big four are creeping up to 4 to 4.5 per cent, which is starting to look attractive again for income investors. The big question is whether this is a buying opportunity or the start of a structural de-rating. We think it's the former: the majors' balance sheets are stronger than they were in 2008, and APRA's 4.5 per cent dividend payout cap is still binding, which means dividends are sustainable even if earnings fall further.

The oil price spike is a near-term inflation risk. If Brent stays above $90 a barrel for another month, expect the RBA's 'transitory' language to harden, and rate-cut expectations to push out.
whatItMeans: If you hold the big four bank stocks: Watch the dividend yields. At 4 to 4.5 per cent, the majors are looking attractive again, but only if you can stomach another 10 per cent drawdown from here.
If you have money in a high-interest savings account: Expect rates to start falling within six months as deposit competition cools. The banks are losing their best growth channel.
If you have a mortgage: Variable rates are unlikely to fall until late 2026 at the earliest. The bank share-price weakness reflects margin pressure, not loan losses.
If you fill up a car: The oil spike will pass through to petrol within four to six weeks. Budget an extra $10 to $15 a tank if it holds.
